healthsia.title: HealthSIA
healthsia.headline: A perioperative care platform adopted across multiple clinics
healthsia.summary: Role-based dashboards, questionnaires, care plans and chat for patients and care teams.

tldr.problem: Surgery care involves surgeons, therapists, nutritionists, clinic staff and the patient. They needed one platform where each role sees only its own data and tools.
tldr.approach: I designed and built role-based dashboards with strict access control, a reusable list pattern, step-by-step wizards, a questionnaire builder and real-time chat.
tldr.impact: Adopted across multiple clinics. API responses got ~40% faster after I optimized database queries and added indexes.

blocks.title: Six roles, one patient journey
body: HealthSIA supports patients before and after surgery. Each patient has a care team of surgeons, therapists and nutritionists, backed by clinic admins and a super admin.

It has two sides: a web console for the care team and administrators, and a mobile app where patients answer questionnaires, follow meal and exercise plans, request appointments and chat with their team.

blocks.title: Each role needed its own view of the same data

items.title: Super admin
items.body: Sets up clinics, admins and specializations, and shared data such as foods and exercises.

items.title: Clinic admins
items.body: Manage their clinic’s physicians, therapists, nutritionists and patients.

items.title: Care team
items.body: Sends questionnaires, plans meals and exercises, and follows up through appointments and chat.

items.title: Patients
items.body: Follow one guided journey in the app, from onboarding questions to the plan after surgery.

blocks.title: Four requirements behind every screen
items: Strict access: every screen and API call limited to the signed-in role.
Multi-phase questionnaires, including surgery questionnaires, with status tracking and reminders.
Appointments that catch scheduling conflicts before they reach a patient.
Real-time chat that still notifies people who are offline.

blocks.title: What I owned
blocks.intro: I worked across design and code. Clinical content — questions, foods, exercises — is managed by admins in the console.
items: UI/UX and front-end of the web console in React and Next.js: dashboards, list and form patterns, wizards, the questionnaire builder.
The Node.js and Express API on MySQL and Sequelize, with JWT authentication and strict role-based access.
Socket.io chat rooms with offline notifications; meal plans, exercise programs and conflict-checked scheduling.
Query optimization and indexes (~40% faster API responses), CI/CD and Google Cloud deployments.

blocks.title: Four decisions that shaped the console

items.title: Choose your role before you sign in
items.problem: Several roles share one console, each with different menus, data and actions.
items.decision: Make the role the first choice at sign-in — Super Admin, Clinical Admin or Physician — so each session opens in the right workspace.
items.tradeoff: One extra step at sign-in. In return, nobody lands in a view meant for someone else.

items.title: One list template for every record
items.problem: Admins manage over a dozen record types, from clinics and staff to foods and questionnaires.
items.decision: One page template everywhere: breadcrumb, search, “+ New”, an Active/Inactive summary and a paged table with row actions.
items.tradeoff: Some records could use a custom layout. Consistency won: admins learn the console once, and new modules ship faster.

items.title: Long records as step-by-step wizards
items.problem: A new nutritionist or therapist needs six kinds of information, from profile and address to permissions and emergency contacts.
items.decision: A vertical six-step wizard: every step visible, one open at a time, each ticked off when complete — and reused for editing.
items.tradeoff: More clicks than one long page, but each step validates on its own and an edit jumps straight to the right step.

items.title: Questionnaires as data, not code
items.problem: Clinics run onboarding, well-being, feedback and surgery questionnaires, and the list keeps growing.
items.decision: A builder where admins pick a category and one of nine question types, from single choice to rating, so new questionnaires need no release.
items.tradeoff: Fixed question types rule out unusual formats. In return every answer is structured, which tracking and reminders rely on.

blocks.title: Two themes, one design language
body: The dashboard leads with counts of patients, surgeons, therapists and nutritionists, each with a trend badge, then surgeries and six months of appointments — in light and dark themes built from the same components.
Lists and detail pages have real empty states, so an empty clinic reads as empty, not broken.

blocks.title: Adopted across multiple clinics
body: I only quote what was measured: the ~40% is API response time after query optimization and new indexes.
I have no usage data to share; adoption across multiple clinics is the clearest sign the workflows hold up in daily use.

blocks.title: Screens from the console and the patient app
With more time I would…
body: Time the most frequent jobs with clinic staff — adding a patient, sending a questionnaire, booking an appointment — so the next decisions rest on evidence.
Document the list, form and wizard patterns as a component library with written states and accessibility checks.

ounlab.title: OunLab (OUN.AI)
ounlab.headline: AI project management with real-time collaboration, live at oun.ai
ounlab.summary: Tasks, files, dashboards and payments for owners and freelancers, with OpenAI built in.

tldr.problem: OUN connects business owners with freelance developers. Both sides needed one place to plan the work, share files, talk in real time and handle payments.
tldr.approach: I designed and built a real-time web app — tasks, dashboards and files over WebSockets, admin and user roles, Stripe payments and OpenAI integration — plus the dark marketing site.
tldr.impact: Live at oun.ai, with the AI assistant greeting visitors on the landing page.

blocks.title: A software-development partner with AI built in
body: OUN.AI (OunLab) is a platform where business owners get software built and freelancers find projects, join teams and get paid. The landing page sums it up: “Reshaping and Innovating Software Development”.
Underneath the marketing site is a project-management SaaS: tasks, files, dashboards and payments, with OpenAI built in.

items.title: Business owners
items.body: Get software built, follow progress on dashboards and pay inside the platform.

items.title: Freelancers
items.body: Find projects, join teams, track their tasks and get paid securely.

items.title: Admins
items.body: Manage users and roles across the platform.

blocks.title: What the workspace had to do
items: Show every change to everyone as it happens, without a refresh.
Keep tasks, files, dashboards and payments in one place.
Offer AI help, starting on the landing page.

blocks.title: What I owned
blocks.intro: I worked across design and code:
items: UI/UX and front-end in React, Next.js and Tailwind CSS: dashboards, task and file views, and the marketing site.
Real-time collaboration over WebSockets, with shared state in Redux Toolkit.
Node.js back-end workflows, admin and user roles, and Stripe payments.
The OpenAI API integration behind the assistant.

items.title: Real-time by default
items.problem: Owners and freelancers work on the same tasks, files and dashboards, often at the same time.
items.decision: Push changes over WebSockets so boards and dashboards update for everyone without a refresh.
items.tradeoff: Persistent connections are harder to scale and test than plain requests. For a collaboration tool, stale screens would cost more.

items.title: Payments where the work lives
items.problem: Freelancers need to trust they’ll be paid; owners want payment tied to the work they commissioned.
items.decision: Build Stripe payments into the product instead of handling them outside it.
items.tradeoff: Payments raise the bar for security and error states. In return the whole project — tasks, files and money — stays in one place.

items.title: Let the AI answer first
items.problem: New visitors arrive unsure whether OUN is for them — as a business owner or as a freelancer.
items.decision: Open the landing page with a working chat panel where OUN AI introduces itself and answers questions, not a static FAQ.
items.tradeoff: Every conversation costs an API call, and the assistant has to be right from the first message. A static page is cheaper but can’t answer the question a visitor actually has.

blocks.title: From design to production
body: The marketing site sets the tone: a dark starfield, a particle globe in blue and gold, three plain reasons to join, and a single call to sign up.
In the app, Tailwind CSS keeps screens consistent and quick to build, and Redux Toolkit holds the shared state that live WebSocket updates change.

blocks.title: What shipped
body: OUN is in beta and I have no usage numbers I can share, so I don’t quote any. What I can point to is what shipped, and the site you can open today.

blocks.title: With more time I would…
body: Test the assistant with both audiences and log the questions it can’t answer, then turn those gaps into clearer onboarding.
Measure how long an owner and a freelancer take to get from sign-up to their first shared project, and design against that number.

workinaus.title: Work in Aus
workinaus.headline: A two-sided job portal for Australia, live at workinaus.com.au
workinaus.summary: Job listings, applications and filtered search for employers and job seekers.

tldr.problem: Job seekers in Australia — including people planning to move there — needed to find relevant jobs quickly, and employers needed to post jobs and receive applications, on one site.
tldr.approach: I designed and built a responsive React and Next.js front end around search: keyword, category and suburb in the hero, quick filter chips, and separate employer and job-seeker journeys.
tldr.impact: Live at workinaus.com.au, with search and filters on Elasticsearch and SEO-friendly pages.

blocks.title: Hiring in Australia, from both sides
body: Work in Aus is a job portal for Australia: job seekers search and apply, and employers post jobs and review applications.
The work covered both journeys: listings, applications, search and filters, authentication and SEO, on a responsive front end.

items.title: Job seekers
items.body: Search by keyword, category and suburb, filter by pay and work type, and apply.

items.title: Employers
items.body: Post jobs and review the applications that come in.

items.title: Newcomers to Australia
items.body: People who want to move to Australia or extend their stay, reached through their own sections on the home page.

blocks.title: What the portal had to get right
items: Relevant results from the first search, filtered by pay type, work type, salary and date posted.
Location down to suburb and postcode, not just the city.
Listings that can be found from search engines, not only from the site’s own search.

blocks.title: What I owned
blocks.intro: I designed and built the front end:
items: UI/UX for the home page, search, job listings and featured jobs.
Employer and job-seeker journeys, including sign-up and login.
Search and filters connected to Elasticsearch.
SEO-friendly pages and a responsive layout in React, Next.js, Redux and Bootstrap.

items.title: Search is the hero
items.problem: Search is the reason people come to a job portal, so it can’t sit below a marketing banner.
items.decision: Put the search panel — keyword, category, suburb and filters — in the hero, over the photo, under a short “Start your journey” headline.
items.tradeoff: Less room above the fold to explain the brand; the promo cards and blogs further down do that job.

items.title: Key filters one tap away
items.problem: Pay and work type often decide whether a job is worth opening, but long filter forms slow people down.
items.decision: Show five filter chips under the search — pay type, work type, minimum salary, maximum salary, date posted — and keep the rest behind “Filters”.
items.tradeoff: Chips take vertical space on small screens, so the row stops at five and everything else waits behind “Filters”.

items.title: Location the way Australians write it
items.problem: A city name alone is too vague to judge a commute.
items.decision: Search by suburb, and show suburb, postcode, region and state on every job card.
items.tradeoff: Longer card details, but “how far is it?” is answered before anyone clicks Apply.

blocks.title: From design to production
body: The front end runs on React and Next.js, with Redux for shared state and Bootstrap for the responsive grid. Search and filters run on Elasticsearch.
Job pages are built to be indexed, so listings can be found from search engines as well as from the site.

blocks.title: Live at workinaus.com.au
body: The portal is live and public. I don’t have traffic or application numbers I can share, so the outcome here is the shipped product, which you can try.

blocks.title: With more time I would…
body: Measure the search funnel — searches, job views, applications — and tune the filter chips to what people actually use.
Run usability tests on the employer side, where posting a job and reviewing applicants are the tasks that matter most.

eduhub.title: EduHub Pak
eduhub.headline: SEO-first education discovery for Pakistan, live at eduhubpak.com
eduhub.summary: Universities, programs, scholarships and admission deadlines in one place.

tldr.problem: Students in Pakistan research universities, programs, scholarships and test dates across many sources. EduHub Pak brings them into one place, and it has to rank in search to reach them.
tldr.approach: I designed and built a Next.js App Router site on headless WordPress: content arrives through WPGraphQL, pages are server-rendered and refreshed with ISR, and a custom Tailwind UI system ties it together.
tldr.impact: Live at eduhubpak.com, with search-friendly pages for universities, programs, scholarships and news.

blocks.title: Everything a student needs to choose, in one place
body: EduHub Pak helps students in Pakistan choose where and what to study. The promise is in the headline: “Find. Compare. Decide — Your Education Journey, Simplified.”
It covers universities and programs with advanced filters, admission deadlines and test dates, a scholarship database with eligibility filters, education news and test-prep resources.

items.title: Find
items.body: One search box with suggested searches, and a university explorer filtered by province, city and type.

items.title: Compare
items.body: The same facts for every university and program, and an admissions tracker with deadlines and test dates.

items.title: Decide
items.body: Scholarships filtered by eligibility, with a University Match Calculator marked as coming next.

blocks.title: What the platform had to handle
items: Content that changes often: admission deadlines, test dates, scholarships and news.
Many content types that must look and behave the same way.
Organic search as a growth channel, so every page has to be indexable.
Editors who publish in WordPress, not in code.

blocks.title: What I owned
blocks.intro: I designed and built the site:
items: UI/UX of the home page, university explorer, admissions tracker and scholarship pages.
A custom UI system on Tailwind CSS, reused across universities, programs, scholarships and news.
The Next.js App Router front end in TypeScript, with SSR and ISR.
The content layer: headless WordPress queried through WPGraphQL.

blocks.title: Decisions behind a findable, easy-to-update site

items.title: Editors keep WordPress; readers get Next.js
items.problem: News, deadlines and scholarships change often and must be easy to publish.
items.decision: Keep WordPress as a headless CMS and render every page in Next.js, pulling content through WPGraphQL.
items.tradeoff: Two systems to run and a GraphQL schema to maintain, in exchange for a familiar editor and a fully custom front end.

items.title: Server-rendered pages that stay current
items.problem: Pages need complete HTML for search engines and quick loads for students, while dates keep changing.
items.decision: Render pages on the server and regenerate them incrementally with ISR as content changes.
items.tradeoff: A page can lag behind the CMS for a short window between regenerations — an acceptable price for speed and indexability on this kind of content.

items.title: Search first, then four clear paths
items.problem: Visitors arrive with different goals: a university, a scholarship, a program, the latest news.
items.decision: Lead with one search box and suggested searches, then four colored tiles: universities, scholarships, programs and news.
items.tradeoff: Four tiles can’t cover everything — test prep and tools sit further down the page — but nobody needs the menu to get started.

blocks.title: From design to production
body: The custom UI system gives universities, programs, scholarships and news the same cards, tables and chips, so the site stays consistent as sections are added.
Pages ship as complete server-rendered HTML that search engines can index, then refresh with ISR when editors update WordPress.

blocks.title: Live at eduhubpak.com
body: The counters on the site — students guided, universities listed — are the client’s figures, not results I can claim. What I can point to is the live platform and pages built to be found.

blocks.title: With more time I would…
body: Finish and test the University Match Calculator with students; matching is where a comparison site becomes a decision tool. It was marked “coming soon” when this was captured.
Validate data between WordPress and the front end, so a missing deadline shows as “to be announced” instead of “Invalid Date”.

shahjee.title: Shah Jee Petroleum
shahjee.headline: Fuel deliveries, QR fuel cards and invoices in one app
shahjee.summary: A fuel-management PWA for admins, clients and delivery staff across branches.

tldr.problem: A fuel distributor needed to track deliveries, fuel cards and payments across branches, clients and suppliers in one system.
tldr.approach: A role-based PWA with QR-code fuel cards, consumption charts, printable receipts and invoices, and a balance sheet.

blocks.title: Fuel operations in one app
body: Shah Jee Petroleum’s system tracks fuel from suppliers to clients across branches. The dashboard leads with counts of admins, clients, branches, delivery persons and transactions, then a petrol-and-diesel consumption chart that filters by admin, client, branch, supplier and date.

blocks.title: What’s inside
items: Four roles: super admin, admin, clients and delivery staff.
QR-code fuel cards, scanned when fuel is delivered.
Printable receipts and invoices, and a balance sheet.
Fuel-consumption charts and totals for petrol and diesel.

blocks.title: What I owned
items: UI/UX and front-end in React, Next.js and Tailwind CSS.
The progressive web app, installable like a native app.
Role-based dashboards, consumption charts, and printable receipts and invoices.

peepskill.title: PeepSkill
peepskill.headline: Athletes, coaches and fans in one sports community
peepskill.summary: A social feed filtered by sport, with live chat, communities, blogs and member roles.

tldr.problem: PeepSkill needed a social home for sport, where athletes, coaches and guests post, follow sports and talk.
tldr.approach: A three-column feed with sport filters, a post composer and trending posts, live chat over WebSockets, communities, blogs and role management.

blocks.title: A social feed organized by sport
body: PeepSkill is a social network for athletes, coaches and fans. The home feed has three columns: sports and followed communities on one side, the feed with sport filters in the middle, and a post composer with trending posts on the other.

blocks.title: What’s inside
items: A feed with sport filters, votes, comments, reposts and sharing.
Live chat and messages.
Communities, blogs and articles.
Roles for athletes, coaches and guests.

blocks.title: What I owned
items: UI/UX and front-end in React, Next.js and Tailwind CSS.
The three-column feed, post composer and live chat interface.
Front-end integration with the Node.js, Express and MySQL back end, and WebSockets for chat.

blocks.title: Courses, browsed like a streaming service
body: Learning Hub is a Udemy-style learning platform. Courses sit in rows by category — development, business and more — with monthly plans and a community around them.

blocks.title: What’s inside
items: Streaming-style rows of courses by category.
Community features: follow, like and comment.
Built-in chat.
Social login and Stripe payments for monthly plans.

blocks.title: What I owned

The streaming-style catalog and course rows.
Community features, chat, social login and Stripe payments.

royalvision.title: Royal Vision Dubai
royalvision.headline: Dubai tours and desert safaris, bookable and payable online
royalvision.summary: A travel catalog with CCAvenue payments and TripAdvisor and Google reviews built in.

tldr.problem: A Dubai tour operator needed to sell tours, safaris and attraction tickets online, and show its TripAdvisor and Google reviews where people decide.
tldr.approach: A responsive catalog with booking, CCAvenue payments, TripAdvisor and Google Reviews integration and SEO, built in React, Next.js, Tailwind CSS and React Query.

blocks.title: From browsing to booked
body: Royal Vision Dubai sells desert safaris, city tours, attraction tickets and holiday packages. The home page opens with a hero slider and one-tap booking on WhatsApp or by phone, then recommended activities with prices in AED.

blocks.title: What’s inside
items: A catalog of tours, activities, tickets and holiday packages.
Online booking with CCAvenue payments.
TripAdvisor and Google reviews on the home page.
SEO and a responsive layout.

blocks.title: What I owned
items: UI/UX and front-end in React, Next.js and Tailwind CSS, with React Query for data.
The booking flow with CCAvenue payments.
TripAdvisor and Google Reviews integration, and SEO.

cover.alt: Royal Vision Dubai home page: winged gold logo, navigation, an “Al Ain Oasis Discovery” hero slide over a lit desert camp, and Book On WhatsApp and Book On Phone Call buttons
cover.caption: The hero slider, with quick booking by WhatsApp or phone.

full.alt: The full Royal Vision Dubai home page: hero, recommended activities with prices in AED, attraction tickets, packages, TripAdvisor and Google review sections, blogs and footer
full.caption: The full home page, from the hero slider to the TripAdvisor and Google review sections.

papaz.title: Papaz Pizza
papaz.headline: A desktop point-of-sale for a pizza restaurant
papaz.summary: Menus, orders and inventory in one Electron app, with staff roles and Stripe.

tldr.problem: A pizza restaurant needed one desktop app for taking orders, managing the menu and tracking stock.
tldr.approach: An Electron app in React and Tailwind CSS: a category-first menu with photo tiles, pending and completed orders, inventory, roles, a dashboard with charts and Stripe payments.
tldr.impact: Built as a desktop app for the restaurant, so there’s no public link.

blocks.title: Big, clear targets for a busy counter
body: Papaz Pizza’s point-of-sale opens on large photo tiles by category — pizzas, kebabs, burgers, drinks, extras — with the cart beside them and tabs for pending and completed orders.

blocks.title: What’s inside
items: A category-first menu with large photo tiles.
Pending and completed orders, and a cart panel.
Inventory tracking and staff roles.
A dashboard with charts, and Stripe payments.

blocks.title: What I owned
items: UI/UX and front-end of the Electron app in React and Tailwind CSS.
The category-first menu, order tabs and cart.
Inventory, staff roles, the charts dashboard and Stripe payments.

cover.alt: Papaz Pizza point-of-sale: a category list on the left and a grid of food photo tiles for pizzas, kebabs, burgers, chicken, drinks and extras

full.alt: The full Papaz Pizza point-of-sale screen: category list, food photo tiles and an empty cart panel on the right
full.caption: The order screen: categories, photo tiles and the cart side by side.

mdhov.title: MDHOV
mdhov.headline: A content-rich website for a Canadian digital agency
mdhov.summary: Service pages, a client showcase, blogs and email inquiries in a responsive build.

tldr.problem: MDHOV, a Canadian agency for web development, design and digital marketing, needed a site that explains many services and makes it easy to get in touch.
tldr.approach: A responsive WordPress site with service pages, a how-it-works section, a client showcase, blogs and email integration, built with HTML5, CSS, Bootstrap, AJAX and Laravel.

blocks.title: Many services, one clear path to contact
body: MDHOV is a Canadian digital agency offering web development, design and digital marketing. Its website presents a wide range of services and keeps contact close: “Let’s Start a Project”, call-back requests and email inquiries. Figures in the agency’s own copy are theirs, not my results.

blocks.title: What’s inside
items: Service pages for web development, SEO and e-commerce.
A four-step “How It Works?” section and a client showcase.
Blogs and articles, with email integration for inquiries.
A responsive layout across devices.

blocks.title: What I owned
items: UI/UX and front-end of the responsive site on WordPress and Laravel, with Bootstrap and AJAX.
Service pages, the how-it-works section and the client showcase.
Blogs and articles, and the email integration for inquiries.

cover.alt: MDHOV agency website hero with a gradient background, a woman leaping out of a smartphone among social-media icons, and service cards below

full.alt: The full MDHOV home page: hero, service cards, web-design features, a how-it-works section, client showcase, inquiry options, integration logos and footer
full.caption: The home page, from services to inquiry options.
